desc:
A single machine runs jobs, where jobs[i] = [duration, weight], one at a time without pauses, starting at time 0 and in any order you choose. If job i finishes at time Ci, it costs weight × Ci.

Return the minimum possible total cost, taken modulo 1,000,000,007 (the minimum is found over the exact values; only the final number is reduced). Return 0 for no jobs.

jobs = [[3, 1], [1, 2]]  ->  6

Running the second job first costs 2 × 1 + 1 × 4 = 6; the other order costs 1 × 3 + 2 × 4 = 11.
hints: Compare just two jobs A and B. Work out the cost of the pair for the order A, B and for B, A, and see what the difference depends on.
The two costs differ by weight(A) × duration(B) versus weight(B) × duration(A). Rewrite this as a comparison of two ratios.
Sort by duration / weight ascending (compare with cross-multiplication to avoid fractions), then accumulate time and cost.
editorial: For two neighbouring jobs A, B starting at time s, the other jobs are unaffected by their order. Doing A first adds wA(s + dA) + wB(s + dA + dB), while B first adds wB(s + dB) + wA(s + dA + dB). A first is better exactly when wB dA < wA dB, i.e. dA / wA < dB / wB.

So sort the jobs by duration / weight in increasing order (Smith's rule) and sum weight × finish. Jobs with equal ratios can be placed in any order without changing the total. The exact total can reach about 1011, which is why the problem asks for it modulo 109+7; Python integers do not overflow so the reduction happens only at the end. Time O(n log n).
solution:
from functools import cmp_to_key


def minWeightedCompletion(jobs):
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    order = sorted(jobs, key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: a[0] * b[1] - b[0] * a[1]))
    t = 0
    total = 0
    for duration, weight in order:
        t += duration
        total += weight * t
    return total % MOD
